options.text: Data survives the loss of one machine
Another machine can take over if one fails

questions.explanation: Copies improve durability, read capacity and availability. Writes don't get faster: they must reach more machines.

questions.prompt: A user edits their bio, reloads, and sees the old bio. Reads go to asynchronous followers. What's happening?

options.text: Replication lag: the follower hasn't received the change yet

questions.explanation: The leader has the new bio, but the follower serving the reload lags behind. Reading a user's own recent writes from the leader fixes it.

questions.prompt: The leader acknowledges writes before any follower has them (asynchronous replication), then crashes. What can happen after failover?

options.text: Nothing; asynchronous replication never loses data
Recent writes that were acknowledged to clients may be lost

questions.explanation: Writes the old leader acknowledged but hadn't yet sent to followers don't exist on the new leader. A synchronous follower prevents this at the cost of slower writes.

questions.prompt: With N = 3 replicas, which settings guarantee a read sees the latest successful write?
questions.explanation: Read and write sets must overlap: R + W > N. 2+2, 3+1 and 1+3 all exceed 3. With 1+1 a read can miss the one replica that took the write.

questions.prompt: During a network glitch, a follower is promoted while the old leader is still running and accepting writes. What is this, and what prevents it?

options.text: Replication lag; prevented by synchronous replication
Split brain; prevented by requiring a majority vote to lead and fencing the old leader so its writes are rejected
A read repair; prevented by anti-entropy

questions.explanation: Two leaders accepting writes is split brain. A leader that can't reach a majority must step down, and fencing tokens make storage reject writes from a deposed leader.
